title: DOC: make plot accessor method docstrings consistent (GH#20348)
BUG: read_parquet/to_parquet fall back to fsspec when pyarrow can't build the filesystem (GH#58078)
body:
closes #58078

With the pyarrow engine and no `storage_options`, `_get_path_or_handle` first tries `pyarrow.fs.FileSystem.from_uri` and falls back to fsspec only on `TypeError`/`ArrowInvalid`. For `hdfs:///path` (empty host, meaning "use `fs.defaultFS` from core-site.xml"), Arrow builds the namenode as `"hdfs://"` and libhdfs raises `OSError`, so the call fails instead of falling back. fsspec's `HadoopFileSystem` handles this URL (it defaults to `host="default"`), which is why the reporter's `storage_options={}` workaround works.

An `OSError` now falls back too, but only for `hdfs:///` URLs (no host): otherwise it is a real error (e.g. `OSError: Bucket '...' not found` from S3), and falling back would replace it with a misleading fsspec/s3fs `ImportError`. If the fsspec fallback also fails, pyarrow's error is chained as its cause. Separately, `ArrowInvalid` is widened to `ArrowException` so that `ArrowNotImplementedError` (pyarrow built without a given filesystem) falls back too. The test registers an in-memory fsspec implementation for `hdfs` and round-trips `hdfs:///...`; pyarrow raises `OSError` there whether or not libhdfs is installed. Other tests check that an `OSError` propagates for other schemes and for `hdfs://` with a host, and that pyarrow's error is chained when fsspec also fails.

title: BUG: raise instead of silently falling back in array strftime (GH#58178)
body:
closes #58178

`DatetimeArray.strftime` (and so `DatetimeIndex.strftime`, `Series.dt.strftime`, and `to_csv(date_format=...)`) caught any `ValueError` from `Timestamp.strftime` and quietly substituted `str(ts)`, giving e.g. `['1820-01-01 00:00:00', '20']` for `%y`. This takes the issue's "always raise" alternative rather than adding an `errors=` keyword. The error now propagates, matching `Timestamp.strftime` and `PeriodArray.strftime` (which already raises `Invalid format string`, GH-53562).

On POSIX, `datetime.strftime` essentially never raises `ValueError`, so this only changes behavior on Windows (`%y` before 1900 on Python < 3.14, directives MSVC doesn't support such as `%-d`). The new test is therefore Windows-only.

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:

`BarPlot._make_plot` fills missing values with `fillna(0)`. On a `timedelta64` column containing `NaT`, the integer `0` upcasts the column to object (now also a `Pandas4Warning`), after which matplotlib raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'numpy.int64' and 'Timedelta'`. Stacked line, `area`, `pie`, and `hist` of timedelta values still raise for unrelated reasons (float/timedelta arithmetic); left out of scope, see also GH-17553.

title: CI: add LeakSanitizer job
body:
closes #66140

Adds a `Clang (ASAN/LSAN)` job that runs the same test selection as the existing ASan/UBSan job, but on a CPython built with ASan (and so without pymalloc), with leak detection on. Instead of building CPython, it uses the prebuilt `ghcr.io/nascheme/cpython-asan:3.14` image (pinned by digest), the same one numpy's LSan job uses, and installs the minimal dependencies with pip. Setup and build take ~7 min and the tests ~29 min at `-n auto`, about the same as the existing sanitizer job.

- pytest-xdist kills workers that take more than 10 s to exit, which an ASan build does after a long run, so LSan's exit-time check never runs in them and the job would pass whatever leaked. `ci/lsan_check.py` runs the check at session end in each worker instead. Reports go to files, and a follow-up step fails the job if any exist.
- The only suppression needed is a CPython float from `os.stat()` that isn't freed at exit (`leak:fill_time`). The suite currently has no other leaks.
- UBSan stays in the existing job. Mixing it in here would put both sanitizers' suppressions through the same runtime.

To check that a leak is caught, I removed the `free` of `line_fields` in `tokenizer.cpp`: the job [failed](https://github.com/jbrockmendel/pandas/actions/runs/36368569602) and reported ~197 MB, all from tokenizer allocation sites. With that reverted it [passes](https://github.com/jbrockmendel/pandas/actions/runs/36371154244).

Limitation: LSan only reports memory nothing points to. A missing `Py_DECREF` on an object that stays alive anyway (as in GH-66115 and GH-66033), or on a GC-tracked object, is invisible to it, so this mainly guards raw allocations in the C code.

title: BUG: where/mask mishandled a list `other` for extension dtypes (GH#63842)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #63842

`ExtensionArray._where` and `._putmask` index `value[~mask]` directly, which only works if `value` is already an ndarray/ExtensionArray of exactly `len(self)`. Nothing upstream converts a plain list, so a list `other` silently fell back to `object` for `str`/`string[pyarrow]`/`interval` and raised `TypeError: only integer scalar arrays can be converted to a scalar index` for `Int64`/`Float64`/`boolean`/`ArrowDtype` — the reported bug is only the string half of that. `Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and boolean-mask setitem are fixed with it, since they route through the same two methods.

The conversion is done in a new `EABackedBlock._align_listlike_arg`, not in `ExtensionArray`. `_where`/`_putmask` keep their existing contract ("arraylike with the same length as self"), so an EA author still reads the same short method, and `EABackedBlock.where`/`.putmask` are their only callers outside the EAs themselves. Handling it at the block level also reaches `NDArrayBackedExtensionArray` and `SparseArray`, which override `_where` so a fix on the base class never applied to them, and the 2-D datetimelike blocks, where a list reached `np.where` unaligned and silently filled **every** masked position with `other[0]`.

A 2-D block now gets one alignment order: one entry per selected position (putmask only — the analogue of the `np.place` call `putmask_without_repeat` makes for numpy dtypes), then one value per column, then one value per row filling every column. A length that fits none of them raises `ValueError`. The order matters because a consolidated `datetime64[ns]`/`timedelta64[ns]` block holds every column of the frame while `Int64`/`ArrowDtype`/`Categorical`/`datetime64[ns, tz]`/`period` get a block each: before this they gave different answers for the same input, and now they agree.

Non-`Sequence` list-likes — `dict`, `set`, `MultiIndex` — are passed through untouched, so the EA holds them as a scalar (the object-backed dtypes) or rejects them (masked, Arrow, `Categorical`), exactly as before. A tuple is likewise left alone: object dtype holds one as a scalar (GH-37681), and `Index.fillna` admits one.

Note on the conversion: it goes through `com.asarray_tuplesafe` rather than `_from_sequence(dtype=self.dtype)`. `_from_sequence` coerces where we need it to raise — `str` turns `9` into `"9"` and `Categorical` turns an unknown category into `NaN` — and it is the setitem call raising that triggers the block's upcast to `object`.

Base extension tests cover the list shapes, xfailed for `SparseArray` (no item assignment) and `JSONArray` (its `__setitem__` mishandles a boolean mask, which is also the cause of the pre-existing `test_where_series` xfail there).

Not reconciled here: 1-D EA dtypes get one block per column, so they cannot see the frame's column count, and a multi-column EA frame still reads a row-length list per column (`df[key] = [10, 20, 30]`) where the numpy and object spellings raise. That needs the rule moved into `NDFrame._where`, which changes behavior for every dtype and belongs in its own PR. The whatsnew entries are scoped to what actually changed.

title: BUG: tz_localize shift onto the NaT sentinel returned a bogus timestamp (GH#66697)
body:
**Stacked on #66820** — the first two commits here are that PR. Only the last commit (`ff3472d`) is new; I'll rebase this down to a single commit once #66820 lands.

Follow-up to GH-66697, which is closed but left one case behind: a timedelta `nonexistent` shift can land the wall time *itself* exactly on the NaT sentinel. `checked_add` does not flag that — the sum fits in an int64 — so it reaches the transition lookup, which has no meaningful answer for a value sorting below every transition. It resolves to the zone's earliest offset and hands back the sentinel shifted by it, silently:

```python
ts = pd.Timestamp("1933-04-30 02:30").as_unit("ns")
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex([ts, ts])
shift = pd.Timedelta(pd.Timestamp.min._value - 1 - ts._value, "ns")

dti.tz_localize("Pacific/Honolulu", nonexistent=shift).asi8
# array([-9223334150854775808, -9223334150854775808])   <- NaT sentinel + LMT offset
```

On `main` — that is, without #66820 underneath — the same input is worse: `delta_idx` goes to `-1` and indexes `info.deltas` off the front of the array. `tz_localize_to_utc` is `boundscheck(False)`/`wraparound(False)`, so that is a raw read of whatever precedes the buffer: `Pacific/Honolulu` returned a timestamp centuries away while `US/Eastern` raised about the shifted value rather than the one the caller passed, and which of the two you get depends on the heap. #66820 removes the out-of-bounds index; this PR rejects the sentinel, which had no business reaching that lookup either way.

The fix raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, naming the caller's wall time, as soon as the shift lands on the sentinel.

No whatsnew entry: the unreleased v3.1.0 bullet for GH-66697 already describes this behaviour ("... instead of raising `OutOfBoundsDatetime` when the shift leaves the representable range"). A second bullet would read as a separate bug.

The test deliberately uses a two-element index. With one element, `DatetimeIndex.tz_localize` boxes element 0 to compare it against `NaT` and raises there of its own accord, which masks whatever `tz_localize_to_utc` actually returned — a single-element version of this test passes on a tree where the bug is fully live.

In the C parser's batched numeric sweep, each column's NA mask was allocated with `np.zeros`. numpy releases the GIL around the `calloc` for anything 1 KiB or larger, so every (column, chunk) pays a GIL release and re-acquire, which is expensive when several parallel `read_csv` workers contend for it. The masks are now allocated with `np.empty` and zeroed inside the sweep's existing `nogil` section.

Measured with the C engine against the parent commit, reading at the usable CPU count (8 on x86, 12 on an M3 Pro), n=12 (macOS n=30), `*` = 95% CI excludes 1.0:

| case | Linux x86 | Windows x86 | macOS arm64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| wide (100 cols), all workers | 1.058x * | 1.026x * | 1.240x * |
| wide (100 cols), default 4 workers | 1.017x | 1.011x * | 1.040x * |
| wide, serial | 0.996x | 1.003x | 0.995x |

Narrow files do not use the sweep and are unchanged. Existing tests cover the zeroing: dropping it fails `test_row_blocked_conversion_late_dtype_miss`.

title: BUG preserve row alignment in grouped resampling on columns
body:
Fixes #59350.

Grouped resampling on a datetime column can assign values to the wrong time bins when row labels differ from row positions:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "group": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=4, freq="min"),
        "value": [100, 200, 1000, 2000],
    },
    index=[1, 0, 3, 2],
)
df.groupby("group").resample("1min", on="date").agg({"value": "sum"})
```

The values for group a come back as 200 then 100 instead of 100 then 200; group b is similarly reversed. Each group now uses a copied time grouper with its cached state cleared. title: BUG: MultiIndex setops split a string operand entry into its elements (GH#39699)
body:
Note: this does **not** close GH-39699, which asks for the opposite change — see the last section.

`MultiIndex._convert_can_do_setop` passes a raw list-like operand straight to `MultiIndex.from_tuples`, which accepts any indexable row and so decomposes a string or bytes entry into its elements. When the entry's length matches `nlevels`, the setop treats it as a tuple of level values:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])
mi.intersection(["ac"])              # MultiIndex([('a', 'c')])  -- "ac" is not in mi
mi.union([b"ac"])                    # adds (97, 99)
mi.intersection([("a", "c"), "bd"])  # "bd" matches ('b', 'd')
```

The four setops now raise the existing `TypeError("other must be a MultiIndex or a list of tuples")` for such an operand. Everything else keeps its existing path through `from_tuples`, including `np.void` rows and null entries, which `lib.to_object_array_tuples` deliberately expands to an all-null row.

Two deliberate behavior changes worth a reviewer's attention:

- Splitting a length-`nlevels` label has two outcomes today — it matches spuriously when the characters line up, and returns the right answer by accident when they don't. Both now raise, so e.g. on 2-level columns `cols.difference(["id"])` returned both columns before and now raises. A deprecation cycle isn't really available, since it would mean continuing to return `('a', 'c')` from `mi.intersection(["ac"])` for another release; the `MultiIndex.isin` change in GH-20252 is the local precedent for going straight to raising.
- On a one-level `MultiIndex` a single-character label used to match. Any longer label already raised.

On GH-39699 itself: it asks for `mi.intersection(["some_col"])` to return an empty index, as it did on 1.1.5. That result was the same split — `"some_col"` became an 8-level MultiIndex, which then intersected to empty. Ten existing assertions pin `TypeError` for a raw list of non-tuples, so raising seemed the consistent reading, and I've left the issue open for that separate question.

title: BUG: convert non-native byteorder to native at construction (GH#53234)

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
closes #53234

Non-native byteorder numeric data (e.g. `>f4` on a little-endian machine) was kept as-is by the Series/DataFrame/Index constructors, so anything reaching a Cython routine raised `ValueError: Big-endian buffer not supported on little-endian compiler` — Index lookups, unique/factorize/value_counts, take/reindex/merge, groupby, window ops, reductions, etc.

This converts to native byteorder at construction (block creation, `Index._ensure_array`, `pd.array` inference), like `DatetimeArray` already does and `Index` did in 1.5. Public functions that accept a raw ndarray (`pd.unique`, `pd.factorize`, `take`) also convert at their Cython boundary. The GH-43042 tests asserting the byteorder is preserved are updated to assert native dtypes with the same values. Also fixes `pd.array` raising `KeyError` on non-native input, and updates the byte-ordering section of the gotchas guide.

closes #54416

Binary ufuncs without an operator equivalent (`np.logical_or`, `np.logaddexp`, ...) aligned their inputs by taking the union of the axes and calling `reindex`, which raises on duplicate labels. The other behavior in the issue (NaN for non-overlapping columns) is the intended alignment enforced in 2.0 (GH-39239).

title: BUG: read_csv() into FloatingArrays converts np.nan into pd.NA, even with distinguish_nan_and_na=True

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

csv = """,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan"""

with pd.option_context("future.distinguish_nan_and_na", True):
    s = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0, dtype={0: str, 1: pd.Float64Dtype()},
                     keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])["x"]
s
```

### Issue Description

Working with data having both `pd.NA` and `np.nan` is possible and, at least until pandas2, it was possible to save such dataframes as CSV in a format that keeps a distinction between the two (see #65227).

However, in the example above pandas fails with:

```
ValueError: Unable to parse string "nan" at position 2
```

The current workaround consists in reading the CSV as string, and manually map its value to floats:
```python
import io
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

csv = """,x
a,1.0
b,
c,nan"""


def convert_nan(val: str):
    match val:
        case "":
            return pd.NA
        case _:
            return np.float64(val) # includes np.nan

with pd.option_context("future.distinguish_nan_and_na", True):
    s1 = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0, dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)["x"]
    s2 = s1.map(convert_nan)
    s3 = s2.convert_dtypes()
s1,s2,s3
```
returns:
```
(a    1.0
 b       
 c    nan
 Name: x, dtype: str,
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: object,
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: Float64)
```

### Expected Behavior

I would expect `read_csv()` to distinguish between `NA` and `NaN` in the columns with `dtype=Float64`. Even more so if `distinguish_nan_and_na=True`.
```
 a     1.0
 b    <NA>
 c     NaN
 Name: x, dtype: Float64
```

Run locally against the pandas nightly wheel 3.1.0.dev0+2043 with pyarrow 25.0.1 and the two changed files applied: `pandas/tests/strings` and `pandas/tests/arrays/string_` give 5612 passed, 0 failed. The new test fails on main (the pyarrow-backed variants raise `ArrowInvalid`) and passes with this change.
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit) — `pre-commit run --files` on both changed files passes every applicable hook locally; pre-commit.ci is green on this PR.
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions — N/A, no new API
- [ ] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature — intentionally omitted: this regression is only on main and hasn't been released yet (same situation as e.g. #61183)

**Root cause.** Since #66339, `ArrowStringArrayMixin._str_zfill` passes `width` straight to `pc.utf8_zfill` for pyarrow >= 21. The Arrow kernel reserves its output buffer based on `width`, so a negative width raises `ArrowInvalid: Negative buffer resize`. `str.zfill` instead returns the string unchanged for any width not larger than the string itself — which is also what the object and python-backed string dtypes do, and what pandas 3.0.x did.

**Fix.** Clamp the width before calling the kernel: `width = max(width, 0)`. `str.zfill` is the identity function for any width <= 0, and `utf8_zfill(width=0)` returns every string unchanged, so the clamped call matches Python semantics exactly. pyarrow's kernel already mirrors `str.zfill` for the remaining edge cases (sign-aware padding for leading `+`/`-`, empty strings, codepoint-based widths, null propagation — all covered by pyarrow's own `test_utf8_zfill`), so no other adjustment is needed. The pyarrow < 21 elementwise path calls `str.zfill` directly and was already correct.

**Tests.** New parametrized `test_zfill_nonpositive_width` (widths -5 / -2 / 0) in `pandas/tests/strings/test_case_justify.py`, executed across all `any_string_dtype` backends and covering signed strings, an empty string, non-ASCII input, and a missing value. On main, the pyarrow-backed variants raise `ArrowInvalid`; with this PR they return the strings unchanged.

**Out of scope.** `str.pad` / `str.center` / `str.ljust` / `str.rjust` raise the same `Negative buffer resize` error for negative widths on pyarrow-backed strings. That behavior predates #66339 (it is present in released 3.0.x), so it is a separate pre-existing inconsistency rather than part of this regression — happy to open a follow-up issue if you'd like it tracked.

title: BUG: avoid segfault in to_json(date_format=iso) on failed allocation …

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
closes #69461

## Summary

`DataFrame.to_json(date_format="iso")` could segfault when the C
encoder's ISO-datetime conversion (`int64ToIso`, `int64ToIsoDuration`,
`PyDateTimeToIso`) failed — e.g. under a failed memory allocation — and
returned `NULL`. The three callbacks that call these helpers
(`NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback`, `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback`,
`PyDateTimeToIsoCallback`) forwarded that `NULL` to the encoder without
setting `enc->errorMsg`, so `ultrajsonenc.c`'s `JT_UTF8` case (which only
checks `errorMsg`) went on to dereference the `NULL` string.

## Fix

- Each of the three callbacks now sets `errorMsg` when the underlying
  conversion returns `NULL`, so the pending `MemoryError`/`ValueError`
  those helpers already raise propagates instead of being ignored.
- Added a defensive `value == NULL` check in `ultrajsonenc.c`'s
  `JT_UTF8` case as a fallback, so any other `getStringValue` callback
  with the same gap fails safely instead of crashing.

## Testing

Verified against the reporter's own repro (an `LD_PRELOAD` shim that
fails a single targeted `malloc` call): the unpatched build segfaults
at the reported call site; the patched build raises `MemoryError`
cleanly instead. Also ran the existing `pandas/tests/io/json/` suite
locally with no regressions.

I did not add an automated regression test — forcing the specific
allocation to fail is done here via an `LD_PRELOAD` shim outside the
Python process, and I couldn't find a portable way to trigger the same
`NULL` path from pure Python/pytest. Happy to add one if a maintainer
can point me to a pattern used for similar allocation-failure paths.

title: DOC: Merge/join treats lists/tuples differently than other list-likes
body:
### 

- [X] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `master` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.merge.html?highlight=merge#pandas.DataFrame.merge

### Documentation problem

The code for merge, and hence join (and other methods?) uses maybe_make_list which treats lists/tuples differently than other list-likes.

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/c4cce9b75b34179edf000314edf708768486fcbb/pandas/core/reshape/merge.py#L638-L640

The current documentation only mentions a list of strings (join) or a list (merge). The special treatment of lists/tuples should be made more explicit.

### Suggested fix for documentation

merge, left_on argument (right_on is similar):

> label, list/tuple of labels, or array-like, optional
> 
> A single label or a list or tuple of labels will be treated as column or index level name(s) to join on in the left DataFrame. Any other array-like or list of array-likes of the length of the left DataFrame are treated as if they are columns.

join, on argument:

> label, list/tuple of labels, or array-like, optional
> 
> A single label or a list or tuple of labels will be treated as column or index level name(s) in the caller to join on the index in other. If multiple values given, the other DataFrame must have a MultiIndex. Passing array-likes other than lists and tuples will be used as the join key if it is not already contained in the calling DataFrame. When not specified, joins index-on-index. Like an Excel VLOOKUP operation.

title: BUG: PeriodIndex partial-string slicing loses anchor on same-resolution labels
body:
Fixes #66571.

Partial-string slicing on a `PeriodIndex` with an anchored freq resolves the string bound one period too early:

```python
pi = pd.period_range("2000Q1", periods=12, freq="Q-FEB")
ser = pd.Series(range(12), index=pi)
ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]
# returns 2000Q4 and 2001Q1 instead of just 2001Q1
```

`_parsed_string_to_bounds` parses the label into a *calendar*-freq `Period` (discarding the anchor month), then converts it back with `asfreq`. When the calendar and anchored quarters don't line up, that round trip spans two periods instead of one. `get_loc` doesn't have this bug because it builds the `Period` directly from `self.freq` for this same case - reused that here.

Ran locally:
```
>>> ser.loc["2001Q1":"2001Q1"]
2001Q1    4
Freq: Q-FEB, dtype: int64
```

Also ran the full `pandas/tests/indexes/period/` suite (476 tests) plus period-related `indexing`/`truncate` tests (193 tests) - all pass.

title: ENH: Cumsum with reset after certain upper/lower boundary is reached.
body:
A cool new feature would be to have a reset value as an argument in the `cumsum` method. So for example if the cumsum value reaches the _lower_ boundary of 0, it resets to 0. Here's an example stolen from [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57510604/perfrom-cumulative-sum-over-a-column-but-reset-to-0-if-sum-become-negative-in-pa/57511154?noredirect=1#comment101490704_57511154) question:

```
df = pd.DataFrame({'Item':'A',
                   'Value':[7,2,-6,-70,8,0]})

  Item  Value
0    A      7
1    A      2
2    A     -6
3    A    -70
4    A      8
5    A      0
```
**Expected output**
```
[7, 9, 3, 0, 8, 8]
```
As you can see, the cumsum restes after it hits `0` or less.

There are some solutions on SO right: 
- [Solution 1](https://stackoverflow.com/a/57511154/9081267)
- [Solution 2](https://stackoverflow.com/a/56905635/9081267) (note: different question, but same problem)
- [Solution 3](https://stackoverflow.com/a/56904650/9081267) (note: different question, but same problem)

I think this would be a nice improvement to the `cumsum` method as an argument for example:
```
df['Value'].cumsum(lower_boundary=0)
```
Somewhat the same as `np.clip` does with the `a_min` and `a_max` arguments.

title: ENH: add Categorical.to_array CategoricalAccessor.to_array and CategoricalIndex.to_array
body:
### Feature Type

- [X] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

A `Categorical` can currently be converted to a numpy array by using the `to_numpy` method. This is fine if the underlying array is a numpy array, but if it is an  `ExtensionArray` it is is not possible to get an `ExtensionArray` from a `Categorical`, except recreating the `ExtensionArray` manually.

For example for `StringArray`:

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> arr = pd.array(["a", pd.NA])
>>> cat = pd.Categorical(arr)
>>> cat.to_numpy()
array(['a', <NA>], dtype=object)  # does not maintain dtype
>>> cat.categories.array[cat.codes]  # manual method for getting the desired array type and dtype
<StringArray>
['a', 'a']
Length: 2, dtype: string
```

### Feature Description

I propose adding a `to_array` method to `Categorical`, `CategoricalAccessor` & `CategoricalIndex`, which will return an array of the appropriate type (numpy array or ExtensionArray) of the same length as the Categorical. It probably should be possible to convert to and from `Categorical`s and `ExtensionArrays`/`numpy.ndarray`s losslessly and this should be tested for.

### Alternative Solutions

The alternative would be to create the underlying array manually, as in the example above.

title: Shared Benchmark suite for Pandas-like projects

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
It would be valuable to have a benchmark suite for Pandas-like projects.  This would help users reasonably compare the performance tradeoffs of different implementations and help developers identify possible performance issues.

There are, I think, a few axes that such a benchmark suite might engage:

1.  Operation type: filters, aggregations, random access, groupby-aggregate, set-index, merge, time series stuff, assignment, uniqueness, ...
2.  Datatype: grouping on ints, floats, strings, categoricals, etc.
3.  Cardinality: Lots of distinct floats, just a few common strings
4.  Data Size: How well do projects scale up?  How well do they scale down?
5.  Cluster size: for those projects for which this is appropriate
6.   (probably lots of other things I'm missing)

Additionally, there are a few projects that I think might benefit from such an endeavor

1.  Pandas itself
2.  Newer pandas developments (whatever gets built on top of arrow memory), which may have enough API compatibility to take advantage of this?
3.  Pandas on Ray (see this nice blogpost: https://rise.cs.berkeley.edu/blog/pandas-on-ray/)
4.  Dask.dataframe
5.  Spark dataframes?  If we can build in API tweaking (which I suspect will be necessary).

Some operational questions:

1.  How does one socially organize such a collection of benchmarks in a sensible way?  My guess is that no one individual is likely to have time to put this together (though I would *love* to be proved wrong here).  The objectives here are somewhat different from what currently lives in `asv_bench/benchmarks`.  
2.  How does one consistently execute such a benchmark?  I was looking at http://pytest-benchmark.readthedocs.io/en/latest 
3.  What challenges are we likely to observe due to the differences in each project?  How do we reasonably work around them?
4.  How do we avoid [developer bias](http://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2017/03/09/biased-benchmarks) when forming benchmarks?
5.  Does anyone have enthusiasm about working on this?

Anyway, those are some thoughts.  Please let me know if this is out of scope for this issue tracker.

title: BUG preserve left index dtype in left joins

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
## Issue

Closes #63371

## Summary?

When two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` first converts them to a common dtype before performing the join. For a `left` join, this can unnecessarily change the dtype of the resulting index.

This PR preserves the dtype of the **left-hand index** for mixed-dtype `left` joins.

The fix applies to one-level indexes across different dtype families, including:

* string
* boolean
* signed and unsigned integers
* nullable integers
* floating-point and nullable floating-point dtypes
* datetime and timezone-aware datetime
* timedelta
* Period
* categorical
* interval
* `RangeIndex`

The original issue was noticed through `Series.str.cat`, where a string index could unexpectedly become an `object` index after alignment. Rather than handling `str.cat` separately, this PR fixes the underlying `Index.join` behavior.

For cases such as incompatible `PeriodIndex`/`DatetimeIndex` joins, the existing behavior is preserved.

## Tests

Added a regression test covering representative one-level index dtypes.

Also updated the existing numeric and `RangeIndex` join tests to reflect the new left-dtype behavior.

## Validation

* Relevant index join tests pass.
* Regression tests for the affected dtypes pass.
* Ruff checks and formatting pass.
* pandas pre-commit checks pass.
* The broader index test suite has one unrelated failure in `TestTZLocalize.test_tz_localize_overflow_tzlocal`.

title: BUG: pandas.array no longer accepts multidimensional data (GH#64280)

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

body:
pandas.array is documented to be 1-dimensional and to raise ValueError for non-1-D input, but passing an explicit NumPy dtype silently returned a 2-D NumpyExtensionArray. Enforce the documented contract at the pandas.array boundary so the explicit-dtype path raises like the other code paths. Internal NumpyExtensionArray 2-D usage (block operations, GH#38073) goes through __init__ and is unaffected.

`pandas.array()` is supposed to return a 1-D array and raise a `ValueError` when the input contains more than one dimension. However, when an explicit NumPy dtype such as `int64` was provided, passing 2-D data could incorrectly return a 2-D `NumpyExtensionArray` instead of raising the expected error.

The fix adds a dimension check in the explicit-dtype construction path. If the resulting array has more than one dimension, `pandas.array()` now correctly raises the documented `ValueError`.

This change does not affect pandas' internal 2-D use cases, since those arrays are created directly through `NumpyExtensionArray.__init__`, which has been left unchanged.

A regression test was also added to `test_nd_raises` to make sure the 2-D case is properly covered. The change was additionally documented in the `v3.1.0.rst` release notes.

While investigating a reported `read_excel` issue with `header=[0, 2]` (GH#66373), I found that reproduction's `.xlsx` attachment was itself corrupted (its `sharedStrings.xml` is missing a string, so two header cells alias to the same value) — the originally reported symptom does not reproduce with a clean file. While investigating I found a genuine, adjacent bug in `BaseExcelReader._parse_sheet` (`pandas/io/excel/_base.py`): for a non-contiguous `header` list, index-name-row detection used `len(header)` instead of `max(header) + 1`, so it inspected the wrong row and could leak index-name text into real index values. This PR fixes that bug, independent of GH#66373's (invalid) report.

Added `test_read_excel_noncontiguous_header_index_names`, parametrized across all Excel engines via the `read_ext`/`tmp_excel` fixtures. Confirmed it fails before the fix and passes after.

title: CI: open an issue when nightly wheel builds keep failing (GH#55903)
body:
closes #55903

Nightly wheel builds regularly stay red for a week or more without anyone noticing. Since Aug 2025 there have been streaks of 7, 10, 12 and 13 consecutive failed nights, and each failed night also skips the nightly upload to scientific-python-nightly-wheels. GitHub's built-in failure email goes only to whoever last edited the cron line.

This adds a `report_failure` job to `wheels.yml` that runs after scheduled builds:
- On a second consecutive failed night it opens `CI: Nightly wheel builds are failing` (labelled `CI`). A single failed night is ignored, so one-off flakes don't open issues.
- While that issue is open, each further failed night adds a comment.
- Each report links the run and lists the failing jobs plus the pytest `FAILED` test IDs taken from the job logs.
- The next passing night closes the issue.

The job needs only `actions: read` and `issues: write`. It can't be run on a PR, so I ran the script under node with a mocked GitHub client against real logs from the 2026-09-19/20 failures (win_arm64, musllinux_aarch64). zizmor and actionlint are clean.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used to research the failure history, write the job, and test the script against mocks.

title: CI: run pandas-stubs tests daily against pandas nightly (GH#54095)
body:
closes #54095

Adds a scheduled workflow that runs the pandas-stubs test suite (which errors on warnings) against the pandas nightly wheel, after the nightly upload in `wheels.yml`. On failure, `scientific-python/issue-from-pytest-log-action` opens or updates a single issue in this repo, so breakage and new warnings from pandas changes show up here instead of being traced back by hand from the pandas-stubs side. It doesn't run on PRs.

Open questions for the pandas-stubs maintainers before this leaves draft:
- File the issue here, in pandas-stubs, or both?
- The job depends on pandas-stubs using poetry and keeping its pytest config at the repo root.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used to write the workflow and validate it with zizmor/actionlint and a local run of its steps.

title: CI: add monthly link check for docs and docstrings
body:
Adds a monthly (and manually triggerable) workflow that runs [lychee](https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee) over `doc/source/**/*.rst` and the docstrings/comments in `pandas/**/*.py{,x}`, including anchor checks. It never fails: results go to the job summary and, outside of PRs, into a single standing `DOC: Broken links in documentation` issue (labelled `Docs`) that later runs update rather than duplicate.

Why lychee rather than reviving `broken-linkcheck.yml` (GH-55246, disabled in GH-56584, removed in GH-62619): Sphinx `linkcheck` needs a full doc build first, while lychee reads the sources directly and takes about a minute. The noise that sank the old job is handled in `.github/lychee.toml`: `whatsnew/` and tests are skipped, 403 (bot-blocking, 109 of 122 were stackoverflow.com) is accepted, and anchors on github.com/support.sas.com are dropped since they only exist after JavaScript runs.

Run locally against main with the four links fixed in GH-69731, this reports 15 broken links, all confirmed real (stale anchors on matplotlib/mypy/pytest/Cython/Wikipedia pages, and dead reference URLs in code comments) — that is what the first issue would contain.

`make.py linkcheck` and `linkcheck_ignore` in `conf.py` are left in place; they can be removed in a follow-up if this lands.

title: DISC: Validating internal docstring presence, completeness and style

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
We currently have guidelines/checks for docstrings https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/contributing_docstring.html  for the api facing methods/functions following the numpydoc docstring guide https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format.html. since we also use sphinx for building the on-line documentation.

Many of our internal functions don't have docstrings and this could be a barrier to new contributions. For the more complex/undocumented internals, I am concerned that this may also affect the sustainability of the project if only a handful of contributors can grok the code.

The pandas docstring guidelines could be considered too heavyweight for internal functions and therefore may be factor in the incomplete coverage of docstrings for internal functions.

title: DOC: document pixi environments and local doctest runs (GH#64847)
body:
Covers the "document how to use pixi to reproduce a CI env locally" item of GH-64847 (the optional build-backends item stays open), and documents how to run doctests locally now that `ci/code_checks.sh` is gone.

- `contributing_environment.rst`: new "Option 3: using pixi" section — pick the CI job's environment, build with `build-pandas`, test with `ci-test-pandas`.
- `contributing_documentation.rst`: said doctests "can be checked with the script above", but the single-page doc build doesn't run examples. Replaced with a working `pytest --doctest-modules ... -k` command. Selecting by `-k` rather than file matters: `Series`/`DataFrame` doctests are collected under `pandas/__init__.py` since their `__module__` is `pandas`.
- `pixi.toml`: `ci-doctests` and `ci-scripts-tests` get `default-environment = "doctests"`; without `-e` they ran in pixi's bare `default` env and failed with `No module named pytest`.

title: ENH: drop_duplicates(consecutive=True) to drop only consecutive duplicates

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
DataFrame.drop_duplicates can be useful to 'sparsify' a frame, requiring less 
memory/storage. However, it doesn't handle the case where a value later reverts
to an earlier value. For example:

```
In [2]: df = pd.DataFrame(index=pd.date_range('20020101', periods=5, freq='D'),
                          data={'poll_support': [0.3, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 0.3]})

In [3]: df
Out[3]:
            poll_support
2002-01-01           0.3
2002-01-02           0.4
2002-01-03           0.4
2002-01-04           0.4
2002-01-05           0.3

In [4]: df.drop_duplicates()
Out[4]:
            poll_support
2002-01-01           0.3
2002-01-02           0.4
```

Would be ideal to be able to do something like:

```
In [4]: df.drop_duplicates(consecutive=True)
Out[4]:
            poll_support
2002-01-01           0.3
2002-01-02           0.4
2002-01-05           0.3
```

This should also be a much faster operation, since you only have to compare each
row with its successor, rather with all other rows.

You can achieve something like this with some shift trickery:

```
In [5]: s1 = df.shift(1)

In [6]: different = (s1 != df) & (s1.notnull() | df.notnull())

In [7]: df.drop(df.index[~different.any(axis=1)], axis=0)
Out[7]:
            poll_support
2002-01-01           0.3
2002-01-02           0.4
2002-01-05           0.3
```

But this is somewhat cumbersome, and allocating the intermediate shifted
frame can be slow (particularly if done via a groupby with a lot of groups).

```
pd.Index([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]).intersection(pd.Index([2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4]))
# Int64Index([2, 2, 3, 3], dtype='int64')

pd.CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]).intersection(pd.CategoricalIndex([2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4]))
# CategoricalIndex([2, 2, 3, 3], categories=[1, 2, 3], ordered=False, dtype='category')
# -> Is this OK or it should have categories=[2, 3]?
```
## union

Doc says "Form the union of two Index objects and sorts if possible". I'm not sure whether the last sentence says "raise error if sort is impossible" or "not sort if impossible"?
- http://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/generated/pandas.Index.union.html

```
pd.Index([1, 2, 4]).union(pd.Index([2, 3, 4]))
# Int64Index([1, 2, 3, 4], dtype='int64')

pd.CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 4]).union(pd.CategoricalIndex([2, 3, 4]))
# CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 4, 3], categories=[1, 2, 3, 4], ordered=False, dtype='category')
# -> Should be sorted?
```

```
pd.Index([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]).union(pd.Index([2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4]))
# InvalidIndexError: Reindexing only valid with uniquely valued Index objects
-> This should results Index([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4])?

pd.CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]).union(pd.CategoricalIndex([2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4]))
# TypeError: type() takes 1 or 3 arguments
# -> should raise understandable error, or Int64Index shouldn't raise (and return unsorted result?)
```
## difference

```
pd.CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 4, 5]).difference(pd.CategoricalIndex([2, 3, 4]))
# Int64Index([1, 5], dtype='int64')
# -> should be CategoricalIndex?
```
## sym_diff

```
pd.CategoricalIndex([1, 2, 4, 5]).sym_diff(pd.CategoricalIndex([2, 4]))
# Int64Index([1, 5], dtype='int64')
# -> should be CategoricalIndex?
```

title: ENH: Add convenience API to summarize null counts grouped by dtype (e.g. df.dtype_nulls.summary())

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

labels.name: Describe/info/etc
labels.description: obj.describe, obj.info, requests for methods that look similar

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Add a small convenience API to provide a quick, per-dtype view of missing values in a DataFrame. The utility should list columns grouped by dtype with null counts and optional null percentages, and return both a one-row-per-dtype summary and a per-dtype detail table (columns + null counts).

This is a diagnostic convenience (similar in spirit to df.info(show_counts=True) but grouped by dtype and returning programmatic output).

### Feature Description

Add a DataFrame accessor that provides a compact, programmatic summary of missing values grouped by column dtype.

@pd.api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("dtype_nulls")
class DtypeNullsAccessor:
    def __init__(self, df):
        self._df = df

    def summary(self, include_pct: bool = True, sort_desc: bool = True):
        """
        Return (summary_df, detail_dict)

        Parameters
        ----------
        include_pct : bool, default True
            Include null_pct columns (percentage of nulls relative to len(df)).
        sort_desc : bool, default True
            Sort per-dtype detail tables by null_count descending when True.

        Returns
        -------
        summary_df : pd.DataFrame
            One row per dtype with columns:
              - dtype : str (dtype string, e.g., 'float64', 'object')
              - n_columns : int
              - cols_with_nulls : int
              - total_nulls : int
              - avg_null_pct : float (if include_pct)
        detail_dict : dict[str, pd.DataFrame]
            Mapping dtype string -> DataFrame listing columns of that dtype with
            columns ['column','null_count','null_pct'?] (null_pct present if include_pct).
        """

Implementation sketch / pseudocode:

nrows = len(df)
per_col = DataFrame({
    "column": df.columns,
    "dtype": df.dtypes.astype(str),
    "null_count": df.isna().sum().values
})
if include_pct:
    per_col["null_pct"] = per_col["null_count"] / (nrows if nrows else 1) * 100

detail = { dtype: g.sort_values("null_count", ascending=not sort_desc).reset_index(drop=True)
           for dtype, g in per_col.groupby("dtype") }

agg = per_col.groupby("dtype").agg(
    n_columns=("column","count"),
    cols_with_nulls=("null_count", lambda s: (s>0).sum()),
    total_nulls=("null_count","sum")
).reset_index()

if include_pct:
    agg["avg_null_pct"] = per_col.groupby("dtype")["null_pct"].mean().values

return agg, detail


Expected behaviour / examples:

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "a": [1, None, 3],
    "b": [None, None, 2.0],
    "c": ["x","y", None],
    "d": [True, False, True]
})
summary, detail = df.dtype_nulls.summary()
### summary: rows for 'float64', 'object', 'bool' with counts and percentages
### detail['float64'] lists columns 'b' and 'a' with null_count and null_pct


### Alternative Solutions

One-liner / ad-hoc: Users can already compute this with a short snippet:

(pd.DataFrame({'dtype': df.dtypes.astype(str), 'nulls': df.isna().sum()})
   .reset_index()
   .groupby('dtype')[['index','nulls']])


### Additional Context

Related design rationale:

This feature is a convenience diagnostic that complements df.info() and profiling packages; it returns programmatic data structures (DataFrames and dict) so downstream tooling and tests can consume results.

title: ENH: Support `tz_convert` on naive timestamps when naive tz specified

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Closing Candidate
labels.description: May be closeable, needs more eyeballs

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

It is quite common to defensively convert-or-assume timestamps to UTC, which means writing something like this:

```python
def my_function(df: pd.Dataframe, time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Dataframe:
    if time.tzinfo is None:
        time = time.tz_localize("UTC")
    else:
        time = time.tz_convert("UTC")
    ...
    return df.assign(time=time)
```

Alternatively an inline if can be used

```python
time = time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")
```

But this is slightly longwinded, so often helper functions are repeated in loads of modules

```python
def _ensure_utc(time: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:
    return (
        time.tz_localize("UTC")
        if time.tz is None
        else time.tz_convert("UTC")
    )
```

My opinion is that neither the rather long if..else expression nor the usually-not-consistently-named helper method are very readable. There can also be challenges around proper typing on the helper method, when support for e.g. series and datetime index is required as well. This feature request is essentially asking for a shorthand that is native to Pandas for this pattern.

### Feature Description

Add a keyword argument to `tz_convert` which specifies how naive timestamps should be interpreted, instead of raising an error:


```python
time = time.tz_convert("UTC", naive_tz="UTC")
```

It would be functionally equivalent to `time.tz_localize("UTC") if time.tz is None else time.tz_convert("UTC")` - just a shorthand. Of course, `tz_convert` on series, datetime index etc should have the same support.

### Alternative Solutions

"Keeping the status quo" is more verbose and works. The feature request is mainly to make the convert-or-assume pattern easier to both write and read.

But some alternatives that go along the same lines:

- Different keyword arg names, e.g. `.tz_convert("UTC", assume_naive="UTC")`
    - Particularly, putting the verb "assume" might be good for clarity of what the arg does. It's just longer so I didn't put it in the main suggestion (I think the main suggestion is clear enough).
- "Policy style" instead of specific tz, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_utc")`, `.tz_convert("UTC", naive="assume_local")`
    - This could have a default of `naive="raise"` which neatly describes the current behaviour correctly while keeping `tz=None` semantics constant. However it obviously loses the ability to set an arbitrary naive timezone to use. 
- Different specific method, e.g. `.tz_ensure("UTC", assume="UTC")`
    - If someone thinks we're changing the semantics of `tz_convert` too hard. I don't think so, but had to be mentioned.

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: iloc setitem wrote the wrong cells on a Copy-on-Write referenced frame (GH#65446)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
Repairs a regression from GH-65864, which is in 3.0.4 and later.

When another object references a `DataFrame`'s values, `BlockManager.setitem` splits the block so only the targeted columns get copied, then re-expresses the caller's column indexer in the new block's coordinates. GH-65864 collapsed any increasing column selection to `slice(None)` and compensated for reordered ones with an array of positions, plus a reshape of the row indexer to `(n, 1)`. Both substitutions change what numpy does: a slice takes the cross product with the row indexer, an array broadcasts against it. So the referenced path could disagree with the unreferenced one in either direction — writing a cross product where the caller asked for an elementwise pairing, or the other way round.

The column indexer now keeps the kind the caller used: an integer stays an integer, a slice stays a slice (reversed if the selection was), `Ellipsis` and `np.newaxis` pass through unchanged, since the new block holds every column in order, and anything else stays an array of positions. The row-indexer reshape goes with it — it was independently wrong, turning an intended broadcast into a cross product whenever `np.ix_` had not already run — and so does the `np.squeeze`, which is only correct for `np.ix_` output; a user-supplied 2-D row key still reaches that spot, and not squeezing it is what makes it match the unreferenced path.

Symptoms fixed, all only when another object holds a reference:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12.0).reshape(4, 3), columns=list("abc"))
ref = df[["a", "b", "c"]]

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::-1] = np.array([100.0, 101.0, 102.0])
# IndexError: shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast
#   together with shapes (2,) (3,)

df.iloc[np.array([1, 0]), range(1, -1, -1)] = 99.0
# silently writes 4 cells; without the reference it writes 2

df.loc[np.array([True, False, True, False]), "c":"a":-1] = 99.0
# IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
```

For the `managers.py` split path the unreferenced path is the oracle: it never enters this code, so referenced-vs-unreferenced is a differential with no shared failure mode. Over 35,728 cases (4 dtypes x 4 frame shapes x 20 row-key spellings x 14 column-key spellings x 7 value shapes, `iloc` and `loc`) `main` diverges in 3,621. The branch's residual divergences are the empty-indexer family, where an early return skips value validation; that predates GH-65864 and is left alone here.

**Depends on GH-68521, which should merge first.** Keeping the column indexer as an array sends 2-D EA blocks (all-`datetime64`/`timedelta64` frames) through the `indexer[::-1]` + `value.T` pair in `EABackedBlock.setitem`, which `slice(None)` had kept them out of. That pair spuriously transposes a 2-D value when both keys are arrays, so on its own this PR would give referenced datetime64 frames the bug unreferenced ones already have (`df.iloc[[2, 0], [0, 2]] = value` writing the transposed cells). GH-68521 fixes it for both. An earlier version of this PR carried its own copy of that fix; it is dropped in favor of GH-68521.

Note for the backport decision: GH-65864 shipped in 3.0.4, so the `IndexError`/`ValueError` families here are live for 3.0.x users. A backport needs GH-68521 as well, for the reason above.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and ran the differential sweeps; reviewed by me.

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray silently truncated a value an integer dtype cannot hold (GH#68638)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(2, 1.5)` returned `[1, 1, 3]` — the replacement landed, truncated toward zero, with no error and no warning. The numpy-backed Series upcasts to float64 and stores 1.5; the masked `Int64` Series raises `TypeError`. Only the arrow-backed one silently corrupted the value.

`ArrowExtensionArray._validate_setitem_value` boxed the value with `pa.scalar(value, type=pa_type)`, which converts unsafely — `pa.scalar(1.5, type=pa.int64())` is `1`. Because that never raised, the block-level machinery above it never engaged and `putmask_inplace` wrote the truncated value.

This rejects a lossy value in `_validate_setitem_value` with `TypeError`, matching `BaseMaskedArray._validate_setitem_value`. `Series`/`DataFrame` now raise; `Index.fillna`/`Index.where`/`Index.putmask` upcast, since `Index` has no column-dtype contract to protect — both matching the nullable integer dtypes.

The check is a deny-list rather than masked's allow-list on purpose: an allow-list would also turn `arr[0] = "x"` from `ArrowInvalid` into `TypeError`, which is a separate change with its own test fallout.

It runs over list-likes as well as scalars. `pa.array` applies a safe cast to a numpy array but not to a Python list, so `arr[:2] = [9.5, 8.5]` truncated exactly as `arr[0] = 1.5` did while `arr[:2] = np.array([9.5, 8.5])` raised `ArrowInvalid` — the same operation, spelled three ways, silently corrupting in two of them. A non-finite `Decimal` and a `Fraction` fold into the same `TypeError` for the same reason. The scan short-circuits on a container whose own dtype is integer or boolean; other containers pay a few extra passes (measured at 1e6 elements: float64 ndarray 4.8 -> 6.0 ms, object-of-ints 27.1 -> 32.9 ms, int64 ndarray unchanged).

The PyArrow-backed `StringDtype` now accepts a PyArrow *string* scalar in setitem and `fillna` (main rejects it), while still rejecting a non-string PyArrow scalar that pyarrow would cast to its string form. `Series.where` with one previously fell back to `object` and stored a character code: `pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype="string[pyarrow]").where([True, False], pa.scalar("xy"))` gave `['a', 121]`.

One behavior change is left unfinished: a 0-d ndarray fill into `Index.where`/`putmask`/`fillna` now raises `ArrowInvalid` after the upcast, where it previously truncated — `_box_pa` cannot box a 0-d ndarray for the widened type. Hoisting the `item_from_zerodim` unwrap out of the integer gate fixes it but regresses `timestamp`/`duration` setitem, so it is left for its own PR.

Adjacent defects found while working on this and deliberately left out: `insert` truncates through `_from_sequence`; `_box_pa_scalar` raises `AttributeError` for a `Timestamp` against a non-matching type; `interpolate`'s linear fast path integer-divides; a dictionary-encoded integer type is not `pa.types.is_integer` and so still truncates.

title: BUG: factorize trusted a pre-encoded pyarrow dictionary

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

body:
`ArrowExtensionArray.factorize` short-circuited when the input was already `pa.dictionary`-typed and returned the stored dictionary as `uniques`. That dictionary is not a factorization of the values the array currently holds: entries can be unreferenced, they can be duplicated, and a null can live in the dictionary rather than in the indices.

So after an ordinary boolean filter, `groupby` invented a group for a value that was no longer in the frame, while `unique`/`value_counts` on the same column disagreed with it:

```python
enc = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).dictionary_encode()
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": pd.array(enc, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(enc.type)), "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
sub = df[df["v"] > 2]

sub.groupby("k", sort=False)["v"].sum()
# k
# a    4
# b    0   <- "b" appears nowhere in `sub`
# c    3
```

A dictionary holding the same value in two slots additionally split that value across two groups, and a null stored in the dictionary could end up in `uniques`.

The fix re-factorizes in index space — dedupe the stored dictionary, map the indices through it, re-encode, take the uniques back out — so it never materializes the decoded values. Decoding instead silently overflows the 32-bit offsets once the values pass 2 GiB, and the following kernel segfaults. Value types that have no `dictionary_encode` or `take` kernel (nested and view types, `float16`) keep the existing behaviour rather than raising — except under `use_na_sentinel=False` with a null in the indices, where keeping the stored dictionary would leave the null in index space and `factorize` would hand back the `-1` that flag promises not to use; that combination re-raises, as `main` does today.

`uniques` now come out in order of first appearance rather than in the stored dictionary's order, which is what every other dtype does and is visible through `groupby(sort=False)`.

Adjacent defects with the same root cause are left alone deliberately: `_factorize_keys` in `merge`, the `Categorical` constructor, and `unique`/`value_counts`/`mode` all read a stored dictionary the same way, and each needs its own change.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and reviewed the branch over several rounds; the index-space approach was chosen after review found the first version segfaulted.

title: BUG: Index.replace raised instead of widening for a value the dtype cannot hold

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
`Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and `Index.insert` all catch a value the current dtype cannot hold, find a common dtype, and retry on it — `where` was aligned with `putmask` deliberately in GH-39412, on the grounds that an Index has no column-dtype contract to protect the way a DataFrame column does.

`Index.replace` was added later (GH-65099, still unreleased) and delegates straight to `Series.replace`, so it never got the retry:

```python
ci = pd.CategoricalIndex(["a", "b", "c"])

ci.where([True, False, True], "z")   # Index(['a', 'z', 'c'], dtype='str')
ci.replace("a", "z")                 # TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical ...
```

The dtypes affected are Categorical, masked and Sparse — the ones whose `Series.replace` raises `TypeError` for a value it cannot hold. Every numpy-backed dtype already widened, because `Series.replace` upcasts there itself.

Four implementation notes:

- Only `TypeError` is caught, not `ValueError` as in `Index.where`: `replace`'s argument validation raises `ValueError`, and no dtype raises it for a value it cannot hold.
- A replacement whose `to_replace` matches nothing is left out of the common dtype, since `Block.replace` skips those pairs rather than widening for them. Matching goes through `mask_missing`, the predicate `Block.replace` itself matches with — a containment check disagrees with it, notably for an ns-resolution `Timestamp` against object.
- An NA `to_replace` is matched against `hasnans`, and needs no re-check after widening.
- Widening can change how `to_replace` compares (a str, or an ns-resolution `Timestamp`, against datetime categories). When it does, the retry re-raises rather than returning data with the replacement silently dropped. On the regex paths there are no matched literals to re-check, so the retry instead re-raises when it replaced nothing — otherwise a `TypeError` raised for some unrelated reason (`mask_missing` crashes comparing datetime categories against a partial datetime string) would come back as an Index whose only change is its dtype.

Not covered: `Sparse` only widens when the value escapes the Sparse family entirely. `replace(1, 5)` still raises, because the widened dtype is Sparse too and `SparseArray.__setitem__` refuses it just the same (GH-21818) — out of scope here. The behaviour is pinned by a test.

Arrow-backed dtypes are out of scope too, pinned by a test alongside the Sparse one: `pyarrow` raises `ArrowInvalid`, a `ValueError` subclass, so the retry never fires for them. Catching it here would not be enough on its own — arrow's `Series.replace` silently no-ops for a value it cannot hold (`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(1, 1.5)` returns the input unchanged), so that path wants fixing before the Index retry can rely on it.

body:
### Feature Type

### Problem Description

I wish I could use the [scatter_matrix](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.plotting.scatter_matrix.html) function to make [hexbin](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hexbin.html) plots

Add a new parameter `nondiagonal` to `scatter_matrix` to support `hexbin` instead of `scatter`

```
def scatter_matrix(...):

    if nondiagonal=="scatter":
        ax.scatter(...)

```

### Additional Context

Nevertheless, the functionality was kept, and the changes to support this feature are a few lines of code.

The quality of the plots can improve significantly. Here's an example with scatter:

title: DEPR: reset_index inferring dtype of object index levels (GH#30517)
body:
closes #30517

`set_index` stopped re-inferring object columns in 2.0 (GH-42870), but `reset_index` still infers object-dtype index levels when moving them into columns, so the `set_index`/`reset_index` round trip jreback asked for in the issue is lossy for ints, floats, bools, strings and datetimes alike.

This deprecates that inference: `reset_index` now emits a `Pandas4Warning` when an object-dtype level comes out with a different dtype, and 4.0 will retain object. Calling `infer_objects` on the index (or on each level of a MultiIndex) before `reset_index` keeps the current result and silences the warning.

Nothing inside pandas triggers the warning (the non-slow suite passes with warnings-as-errors). Two tests that incidentally built object-dtype string indexes had the `dtype=object` dropped, since neither is about dtypes.

title: CI: Notifications when a job in GitHub Actions fails
body:
xref #32279

For what I see, when a build in the CI for a commit to master fails, only the user who triggered the action receives an alert (assuming the user has notifications enabled in [their settings](https://github.com/settings/notifications#github-actions-heading)).

I think for Travis and pipelines, some people are receiving notifications for all the failures. Ideally we would like to be able to do the same for actions. I had a quick look, but not sure how this can be enabled. I checked in the settings, but no option seems to exist.

title: CI: Write GHA failed builds summary as a GitHub comment

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
I think it'd safe us a significant amount of time, if when a build fails, we get a nice github comment with the problems. The same idea as what pep8speaks does for linting, but for most things.

I think in some cases it'll save us from having to navigate to the logs (which in azure is even more complex than needed, see #26895).

In the cases when we still need to go to the logs for full tracebacks or whatever, we should be able to have direct links to the log in the comment.

For first-time contributors, the comment will generate an email with the exact problem, and they should be able to follow up and leave the CI green without our intervention. This can be very useful for changes to the docstrings. So, when we go and review PRs, there are no formatting mistakes...

Ideally, azure-pipelines should provide it, for them would be quite trivial to implement, since they can get the permissions to add comments as a GitHub app. I created https://github.com/microsoft/azure-pipelines-tasks/issues/10665 and ask PMs couple of times, but doesn't seem this will happen.

The alternative is a bit trickier, which is having a small web app (like 100 lines long flask script) in a server, and add a webhook that calls it after the build finishes (this can be done from either github or azure). The app can do a REST call to azure to get the log content, and the rest should be a simple regex to get the errors.

Let me know if anyone thinks this is not a good idea, or you know of a better solution. For Travis there seems to be an app that does this (or something similar), https://www.travisbuddy.com/, but I'm not sure if there is something for azure.

title: BUG: tz_convert/tz_localize failing or silently wrong with a ZoneInfo built by from_file (GH#64379)

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
GH-64379 routed every `zoneinfo` timezone through a transition cache that rebuilds the pure-python `ZoneInfo` from `tz.key`. That key only describes the object when it was loaded from the installed tzdata under that key — which is exactly what `ZoneInfo.from_file` need not do. Four ways it goes wrong today:

```python
data = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/US/Eastern", "rb").read()
naive = pd.date_range("2025-06-15", periods=3, freq="h")

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data)))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key="my/custom"))
# ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key my/custom'

naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(data), key=5))
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

tokyo = open("/usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Tokyo", "rb").read()
naive.tz_localize(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo.from_file(io.BytesIO(tokyo), key="US/Eastern"))
# silently uses the installed US/Eastern rules; wrong by 13 hours
```

The last one is the nastiest: it's silent, and it's the realistic case, since pinning a tzdb release via `from_file` under the correct key is a large part of why `from_file` exists. `date_range(..., tz=tz)`, `Timestamp.tz_localize` and the `Series.dt` counterparts all follow the same paths.

## Fix

Gate the fast path on whether `tz.key` is a usable handle at all, rather than assuming it is. `get_zoneinfo_twin` returns a verified pure-python twin or `None`, memoized in a `WeakKeyDictionary` so `from_file` objects don't pin entries; `tz_cache_key`, `is_fixed_offset` and `Localizer.__cinit__` all consult it. When there is no twin, values go down the tzinfo-API path that other zones already use past their last cached transition — no new conversion code.

The test for "was this built by `from_file`" is to ask the object to pickle. The stdlib documents that a `from_file` `ZoneInfo` cannot be pickled, for precisely the reason its key is not a usable handle: the data is not recoverable from the key. So a `__reduce__` that raises `PicklingError` means fall back, and one that succeeds means the object came from the installed tzdata under its key. That is an exact test rather than a heuristic, so `ZoneInfo(key)` and `no_cache(key)` both keep the full fast path and are unaffected.

The cost is that a `from_file` object whose data *does* match the zone its key names cannot be told apart from one whose data does not, so it takes the fallback too — correct, but slower (roughly 30x on a large `tz_localize`; 3ms vs 106ms for 100k values here), and without the fixed-offset shortcut in `DatetimeIndex` set operations, so an empty `intersection` comes back with `freq=None`. Anyone who needs both a non-default tzdb and the fast path can point `zoneinfo.reset_tzpath()` at that release *before the first conversion* and load by key — neither the stdlib’s `ZoneInfo` cache nor pandas’ transition cache is invalidated afterwards.

An earlier revision of this PR tried to close that gap, verifying a candidate twin by probing its transitions and a monthly grid — 0 false rejects across all 598 installed zones, but ~120 lines and a documented residual hole before each zone's first transition. Per review it was dropped in favour of the exact-but-coarser test above; the [commit](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/66828/commits/e8a05a8a8f39c27a6a92c0db4d0685066dff8138) is kept for the record.

`tzdata` stays a Windows-only pixi target. The tests here read a known tzdb file off `zoneinfo.TZPATH`, and fall back to `importorskip("tzdata")` only when the zone is not on `TZPATH` at all — in practice Windows, where `TZPATH` is empty and `tzdata` is already installed. `validate_test_dependencies` cannot see `[target.win.dependencies]`, so it gets an allowlist entry saying why.

The other half of the report this came from — wrong offsets for `Africa/Casablanca`/`Africa/El_Aaiun` in 2088-2099 — is **not** live; GH-65712 and GH-65733 already fixed it. Re-checked against the stdlib across all 598 IANA zones for 2020-2099 (`tz_convert` and `tz_localize`, exact) plus a synthetic reverse-DST zone, so nothing is added for it here.

title: BUG: iloc/loc setitem broadcast a 1-D value down rows on an all-datetimelike frame

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
`EABackedBlock.setitem` adapted a 2-D EA block's `(ncols, nrows)` storage layout by swapping the two entries of the indexer tuple rather than transposing `values`, since `EA.T` may not be a view (GH-45419). It reoriented only a 2-D ndarray value to match, so a **1-D value was broadcast down rows instead of across the selected columns**:

```python
arr = np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3).astype("i8")
df = pd.DataFrame(arr.view("M8[s]"), columns=list("abc"))

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::2] = np.array([100, 101], dtype="i8").view("M8[s]")
# each value lands in the wrong column, silently:
#   a=101, c=101 in row 0 and a=100, c=100 in row 2
#   expected (and what a float64 frame does): a=100, c=101 in both rows
```

Where the selection could not absorb the misplaced value it raised instead, as `OutOfBoundsDatetime: Incompatible (high-resolution) value` — the `coerce_to_target_dtype(..., raise_on_upcast=True)` fallback reporting a swallowed shape `ValueError` as a resolution problem. The swap was also wrong in other ways: with two list keys or two masks the indexer entries broadcast against each other, so the swap is not a transpose at all, and `Ellipsis`, `np.newaxis`, trailing commas, 2-D keys and non-ndarray values each needed their own handling.

Every 2-D block in pandas is an `NDArrayBackedExtensionBlock` (datetime64, timedelta64, tz-aware, period), whose `.T` is a view. Those now write through `values.T` with the key in frame order, so numpy does the broadcasting and all of the cases above come out the way they do on a NumPy-backed frame. The indexer swap stays as the fallback for a third-party 2-D EA.

When the value genuinely cannot be broadcast, a 2-D block now raises `ValueError: could not broadcast input array from shape ... into shape ...` in frame order, rather than the resolution error.

`test_iloc_setitem_2d_ea_block_matches_numeric` checks this against a NumPy-backed frame over row key × column key × value shape (plus `np.newaxis`, trailing-comma, `range` and 2-D keys) for all four dtypes: 88 of its 144 cases fail on main.

Behavior changes worth calling out, each making an all-datetimelike frame accept or reject what a NumPy-backed frame does:
- an empty value into an empty *row* selection (`df.iloc[[]] = np.array([])`) was a no-op and now raises; into an empty *column* selection it went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to a no-op;
- a column vector into a single column (`df.iloc[mask, 0] = value.reshape(4, 1)`) used to succeed, because the swap's `.T` turned it into a row vector, and now raises; a row vector into a single row (`df.iloc[1] = value.reshape(1, 3)`) went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to writing.

Scope notes, pre-existing and left alone:
- `df.iloc[1, 1] = np.array([x])` still raises where a NumPy-backed frame writes;
- a 1-D block reports a shape failure through the same upcast fallback, as `TypeError: Invalid value ...` or `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. Giving it the new message would change the exception type of `Series` setitem, which wants its own PR.

title: Configure CI to fail on skip of optional deps?

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

body:
We have a recurring problem where tests are skipped without us realizing. See the discussion on https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/26852 and elsewhere.

Can we think of a way to make this more robust? Perhaps by adding an additional command line option to our pytest calls

```
pytest pandas --no-skip-xclip
```

Then we would update our calls to `pytest.importorskip` to use a pandas' wrapper that checks the config options. By default, it'll still skip, but if the `--no-skip-{dep}` flag is passed we would fail.

This would complicate the actual `pytest` call in the CI scripts, though it's already quite complicated.

title: BUG: Timestamp rejected fold with positional date components (GH#52117)
body:
closes #52117

`Timestamp.__new__` validates `fold` before the `if/elif` chain that decides which of the three calling forms is in play. The guard accepted only the keyword-component form or a naive datetime, so the *positional* by-component form — where `ts_input` holds the integer year — fell through to the "possibly unambiguous input" error, whose own advice is to build from components:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
ValueError: Cannot pass fold with possibly unambiguous input: ...
>>> pd.Timestamp(year=2020, month=1, day=1, hour=0, minute=0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')
```

The fix exempts that form too, keyed on both leading arguments being integers rather than on `year` alone, so the guard cannot admit an input the dispatch chain routes to an earlier arm (null-like, `float` and `bool` first arguments all reach `elif` arms above the positional one).

This also removes a limitation GH-31930 documented in the 3.1.0 whatsnew: `datetime.__replace__` reconstructs subclasses through the 8-positional-argument form and passes `fold` when it is nonzero, so `copy.replace()` raised on any `fold=1` timestamp. That clause is deleted and the test pinning it now pins the fixed behavior.

title: BUG: keep left/right index dtype in Index.join on mismatched dtypes (GH#63371)

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

body:
closes #63371

When the two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` casts both to a common dtype and returned the result in that dtype even for `how="left"`/`"right"`, where every value comes from one side. The join still runs in the common dtype; the result is now rebuilt from the kept side via its indexer, so it keeps that side's dtype (including 1-to-many joins). `inner`/`outer` are unchanged.

This follows the thread's consensus to fix left joins generally rather than special-casing `str.cat`, and carries through `align`, `DataFrame.join`, `merge` and `str.cat`. It also removes an asymmetry where `ser1.align(ser2, join="left")` gave a `str` index on one result and `object` on the other. The empty-index path already kept the left dtype.

Behavior change: 14 existing tests asserted the old cast and are updated.

title: BUG: name the value_labels key in the non-unique Stata labels error (GH#54590)
body:
closes #54590

The "Value labels for column X are not unique" error named only the column, but `StataReader.value_labels()` is keyed by value label set name, which in Stata-written files often differs from the column name (e.g. column `ethnicsn` uses the set `ETHNICSN` in `stata15.dta`). The message now gives that key. The `value_labels` docstring also said the keys are variable names; it now says they are value label names.

title: BUG: to_csv with quoting wrote float32 values with float64 repr (GH#60699)
body:
closes #60699

With `quoting` other than `QUOTE_MINIMAL`, `get_values_for_csv` casts float columns to object so `csv.writer` sees numbers (and leaves them unquoted under `QUOTE_NONNUMERIC`). That cast turns `float16`/`float32` values into Python floats, which are written with the float64 repr: `8.569999694824219` instead of `8.57`.

This keeps them as numpy scalars instead; `csv.writer` still treats them as numeric and writes their `str()`, matching the default-quoting output. Masked (`Float32`) and pyarrow (`float32[pyarrow]`) arrays are converted to numpy first so they get the same treatment. float64 is unchanged.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5.5 (high)`), used to investigate the issue, write the fix and test, and draft this description.
